name: Moses
info: Moses is the Hebrew prophet who, according to the Book of Exodus, led the Israelites out of slavery in Egypt and received the Mosaic Law, which forms part of the Torah. He is revered across the Abrahamic religions.

facts.born: In Egypt, to Amram of the tribe of Levi and Jochebed, according to the Book of Exodus; the Seder Olam Rabbah calculates 1391 BCE
facts.died: On Mount Nebo, in sight of the Promised Land, at the age of 120, according to Deuteronomy; the Seder Olam Rabbah calculates 1271 BCE; his burial place is unknown to the Bible, and Islamic tradition places it near Jericho
facts.role: Prophet, deliverer of Israel from Egypt and lawgiver, held by Jewish tradition to be the greatest of the prophets; most scholars see the biblical figure as legendary, with a Moses-like figure possible
facts.known: leading the Exodus from Egypt; the Ten Plagues and the crossing of the Red Sea; receiving the Ten Commandments at Mount Sinai; the covenant and the Tabernacle; forty years in the wilderness; traditional authorship of the Torah; a prophet in Judaism, Christianity, Islam and the Baháʼí Faith

t: According to the Book of Exodus, Moses was born to an enslaved people, raised in Pharaoh's household and sent by God to bring the Israelites out of Egypt.
At Mount Sinai he received the Ten Commandments and delivered the laws and the covenant that Jews know as the Torah, which tradition has long held him to have written.

Most scholars regard the biblical Moses as a legendary figure while leaving open that Moses or a Moses-like figure lived in the 13th century BCE; no source outside the tradition points to him clearly.
dyk: In Jewish tradition Moses died at 120, with his eye undimmed and his vigour unabated, which is why the phrase "may you live to 120" has become a common blessing.
ev: Moses is born to Amram and Jochebed and hidden in the bulrushes of the Nile, by the Seder Olam Rabbah's reckoning
After killing an Egyptian who was beating a Hebrew, Moses flees to Midian and marries Zipporah
God appears to Moses as a burning bush and commands him to bring the Israelites out of bondage
After the Ten Plagues Moses leads the Israelites out of Egypt and across the Red Sea
Moses receives the Ten Commandments and the Israelites enter the covenant
The Israelites, afraid of Canaan's inhabitants, are condemned to wander for forty years
Moses delivers God's laws, passes his authority to Joshua and dies on Mount Nebo aged 120

sections.early:
Moses is known chiefly from the books of Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers and Deuteronomy. According to the Book of Exodus, he was born in Egypt to Amram, a son or descendant of Kehath the Levite, and Jochebed, who was kin to Kehath. His sister Miriam was seven years older and his brother Aaron three years older. The Israelites had settled in the Land of Goshen in the time of Joseph and Jacob, and a new Pharaoh now oppressed them. When Pharaoh ordered that every newborn Hebrew boy be drowned in the Nile, Jochebed placed her son in an ark and hid it in the bulrushes by the riverbank. Pharaoh's daughter found him, adopted him and raised him as an Egyptian.

The name has been linked to the Egyptian root msy ('child of'), which appears in the names Thutmose and Ramose. Exodus gives it a Hebrew explanation instead, in the words "I drew him out of the water". Kenneth Kitchen and Thomas Schneider hold that the Hebrew origin is the more likely.

Scholars hold different opinions on whether Moses lived. According to William G. Dever, the modern scholarly consensus is that the biblical Moses is largely mythical, though a Moses-like figure may have existed in the mid to late 13th century BCE. The authors of Seder Olam Rabbah calculated a lifespan corresponding to 1391 to 1271 BCE, and the years used here follow that traditional reckoning. The story of a child set afloat in a basket has a parallel in the account of Sargon of Akkad.
sections.rise:
According to Exodus, Moses reached adulthood and killed an Egyptian who was beating a Hebrew. To escape Pharaoh's death penalty he fled to Midian, a desert country south of Judah, where he married Zipporah. On Mount Horeb, God appeared to him as a burning bush, revealed his name and commanded him to return to Egypt and bring his chosen people out of bondage and into the Promised Land of Canaan.

Moses objected that he could not speak eloquently, and God allowed his elder brother Aaron to speak for him. On the journey, the book relates, God tried to kill Moses for failing to circumcise his son, and Zipporah saved his life. In Egypt, Pharaoh refused the demand, and only after the ten plagues did he relent. Moses led the Israelites to the border of Egypt, where, in the account, God hardened Pharaoh's heart once more and destroyed Pharaoh and his army at the Red Sea crossing as a sign of his power.

A theory developed by Cornelis Tiele in 1872 held that Yahweh was a Midianite god introduced to the Israelites by Moses, whose father-in-law Jethro was a Midianite priest. Against it stands the modern consensus that most of the Israelites were native to Palestine. Rudolf Smend argues that the two details about Moses most likely to be historical are his Egyptian name and his marriage to a Midianite woman, which the Israelites are unlikely to have invented.
sections.deeds:
After defeating the Amalekites at Rephidim, Moses led the Israelites to Mount Sinai, where, according to Exodus, he received the Ten Commandments from God, written on stone tablets. Moses and the elders entered into a covenant by which Israel would become the people of YHWH, obeying his laws, and YHWH would be their god. Moses delivered the laws of God to Israel, instituted the priesthood under the sons of his brother Aaron, and received instructions for the Tabernacle, the mobile shrine by which God would travel with Israel to the Promised Land.

Jews honour him as the lawgiver of Israel. The Covenant Code, which embeds the Decalogue (Exodus 20:1 to 17) and the Book of the Covenant, is the first of several sets of laws in the Torah; the books of Leviticus and Numbers are a second body of law and Deuteronomy a third. Moses has traditionally been regarded as the author of the Torah, the first section of the Hebrew Bible.

From Sinai he led the people to the Desert of Paran on the border of Canaan and sent twelve spies into the land. When the people refused to enter, he told them they would wander in the wilderness for forty years until that generation had died. After the forty years the Israelites went east around the Dead Sea to Edom and Moab and, in the account, conquered the lands of Og and Sihon in Transjordan.
sections.opponents:
The Torah itself records opposition. While Moses was on Sinai some of the people feared he was dead and made a golden calf; in anger he broke the tablets and ordered the elimination of those who had worshipped it. After the spies' report some rebelled against Moses and against God and wanted to return to Egypt, and Korah was punished for leading a revolt. Moses also, in the account, massacred the Midianites, whom the Israelites had come to regard as enemies for enticing them to sin. Rabbi Joel Grossman and Alan Levin read the story as a cautionary tale, while the linguist Keith Allan remarked that such behaviour would be tabooed today and might lead to a war crimes trial.

Historians dispute the sources. Jan Assmann argues that it cannot be known whether Moses lived, since no Egyptian source mentions him before the fourth century BCE and no archaeological evidence has been found in Egypt or Sinai. Others, including the Oxford Companion to the Bible, hold that his absence would leave a vacuum that cannot be explained. Martin Noth saw Moses as a late narrative device joining originally separate themes. The Hellenistic writer Manetho, as Josephus summarises him, told of an Egyptian priest, Osarseph, who led an army of lepers and later took the name Moses, and Tacitus has Moses leading outcasts banished by Pharaoh Bocchoris.
sections.last:
According to Numbers, Moses was twice told that he would die before entering the Promised Land: once after seeing it from a viewpoint on Mount Abarim, and again once the battle with the Midianites had been won. On the banks of the Jordan, in sight of the land, he assembled the tribes, recalled their wanderings and delivered the laws by which they must live there. He sang a song of praise, in the account, pronounced a blessing on the people and passed his authority to Joshua, under whom they would possess the land.

Moses then went up Mount Nebo, looked over the Promised Land and died at the age of 120. Deuteronomy says that God buried him in the valley in the land of Moab, opposite Beth-Peor, but that no man knows his burial place to this day, and that his eye had not dimmed nor his vigour diminished. According to some Islamic tradition Moses is buried at Maqam El-Nabi Musa, near Jericho. Members of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints believe that he was taken to heaven without having tasted death. Muslim tradition also records, in a hadith about the life of Muhammad, a meeting in heaven between Moses and Muhammad, which resulted in Muslims observing five daily prayers.
sections.legacy:
Jewish tradition considers Moses the greatest prophet who ever lived, known to Orthodox Jews as Moshe Rabbenu, 'Our Leader Moses', while stressing that he was a human being and is not to be worshipped. He is honoured as a prophet in Judaism and Samaritanism, and the Conservative movement's Torah commentary calls it irrelevant whether the historical Moses existed. In Christianity, Moses is mentioned more often in the New Testament than any other Old Testament figure, is often a symbol of God's law, and is read through typology as a forerunner of Jesus; the Synoptic Gospels have him meet Jesus at the Transfiguration. Several churches commemorate him as a saint on 4 September.

The Quran mentions Moses more than any other individual, calling him both prophet (nabi) and messenger (rasul). The Baháʼí Faith counts him a Manifestation of God and the Druze faith one of seven prophets.

Ancient authors, among them Hecataeus, Strabo, Josephus and Justin Martyr, wrote of him, and Longinus called him the lawgiver of the Jews. Later, several United States presidents, from Harry S. Truman to Barack Obama, used his symbolism, and William Barclay described the Ten Commandments as the law without which nationhood is impossible.

summary: Moses is the figure the Book of Exodus portrays as leading the Israelites out of slavery in Egypt and giving them the Law at Mount Sinai. Most scholars see him as largely legendary, while the faiths that revere him hold him a prophet and lawgiver of great importance.
